Argument Mapper Help

Build an argument

Start with a main contention. Select a box to add support, an objection, or a weak objection beneath it. Co-premises work together in one inference; separate child groups form separate arguments. Double-click a box to edit it. Right-click for more actions; on touch screens, press and hold.

Main argument — white (dark gray in light theme)
Objection — red
Rebuttal to an objection — orange
Weak objection or rebuttal — dashed

Supports inherit their argument’s color. A weak challenge questions whether a claim is established, without establishing its opposite. Notes are annotations, not premises.

Check the logic

Turn on Deductive to check one inference at a time. A rule tag means the conclusion follows from the stated premises; it does not certify their truth. Not recognized means the checker cannot certify the step. Click a canvas tag for details.

Symbolic precedence, tightest first: ~, &, ∨, →, ↔. Conditionals associate to the right. Use parentheses to make grouping and quantifier scope explicit. In English they group too, and so do both … and, either … or and neither … nor: if P, then both Q and R, either P or Q, and R. Where the words leave the grouping open — P iff Q iff R, if P, then Q iff R, necessarily, P iff Q, a list of three after then — the box is marked ? ambiguous. Numbering says where a list begins: if P, then (1) A, (2) B, and (3) C.

A box holds one claim. Because, since, therefore, so, hence and their like put a reason inside a box (P because Q), a whole inference (P, so Q), or a claim that says it was inferred (therefore P). Such a box is marked ✗, and no step with it is checked: give the reason a box of its own below, or leave the word out. Given that may mean because or if, so it is marked ? for you to say which.

A step needs a reason. An objection whose only premise states the denial of the box it objects to is marked ✗ bare denial, and a support whose only premise repeats its box ✗ restates its box: give the reasons as their premises. A weak objection whose only premise says that its box has not been established is marked ✗ bare challenge: a challenge needs reasons too — “If we lack reasons to think that P, then we can’t conclude that P” and “We lack reasons to think that P” give it by modus ponens. None of these carries any force in the verdict unless its box is argued for below it: then its step is ✓ argued below, and stands or falls with that argument. One that is not argued for needs no answer: a rebuttal of it has nothing to rebut, and is marked ✗ nothing to rebut (an objection to a restatement, ✗ nothing to object to), with no force either.

Some boxes ask before their steps are checked. A generic — Mosquitoes carry malaria, A raven is black, or a raven in an if-clause — may mean all of them, some, most, or what holds in general with exceptions. Where the answer decides whether a step follows (Mosquitoes carry malaria and Bob is a mosquito, so Bob carries malaria), the tag says ? generic, and clicking it writes your answer into the box; where the step follows whatever it means, nothing is asked. (Nor where a kind is spoken of: zombies are possible.) A slip of agreement — conscious mental occurrences causes … — is marked ? grammar, with the verb or the noun made to agree for you to choose.

In a conditional with would, the would belongs to the if: from If she knew everything, she would not be surprised and She is surprised, modus tollens gives She does not know everything. Knew after if is read as the present; for the past write had known, and the step offers that reading where it is the one that works. Said alone, She would not be surprised keeps its would; should in its place hedges or says what ought to be, and She is surprised refutes neither. She is not surprised when she leaves denies She is surprised when she leaves.

The Standard basis is Hilbert’s: the axioms shown in the Logic panel, every universal closure of one, and modus ponens as the only rule — enough for every valid first-order argument. Every other rule is derivable from it and is a step the Logic panel can switch off; the familiar ones are on: the classical rules of inference and replacement, the fifteen valid categorical syllogisms, quantifier negation, the rules of passage, and identity. Any rule also applies under a quantifier its premises share with the conclusion (modus ponens under ∀), and a conditional that states a rule’s step, universally quantified or not, needs no support: ∀x ((F(x) ∧ G(x)) → F(x)).

A pronoun is read as the one name its own box gives, and the box says so — not inside what somebody believes or says, and not where two genders mean two people. Poe is Edgar and Dr. Jekyll is Mr. Hyde are identities; Ada is the winner is not, since a description is no second name. A name never goes into what somebody believes, what might be, or what is said of the name itself.

Qualifiers are kept. Probably, likely, presumably, might and perhaps P say that P’s denial is not established; possibly is flagged. Apparently, allegedly, according to Bob, in Hamlet and the like make the sentence one claim. Bob thinks that P is a claim about Bob. Moving a phrase (Q, if P; P, probably; P, Bob thinks) leaves the claim as it was.

Adjectives split where they say something of the thing itself: Poe is a black raven is Poe is black and Poe is a raven. A good pianist is a pianist but may be good only as one, a fake gun need not be a gun, and a word the checker does not know (a zombie argument) is read whole; a step that needs such a phrase split is marked ? ambiguous. Clicking a ? ambiguous tag lists the readings, says which one the step needs, and writes the one you pick into the box (undo puts the old words back). Quantifier words inside a predicate are logic too: loves every raven is loves all ravens, and with Fido is a raven gives Poe loves Fido (not past a modal, a denial, the past, or a verb like seeks).

✓ Warranted means the contention is established by the argument as presented; ✗ Unwarranted can mean missing support or an unresolved challenge, not that the contention is false.

Reuse premises

Choose Add Cross-Reference… from a box’s menu, then click the original premise. Open the badge and drag references together to form an argument; right-click to set its type or include children. Drag a premise into Ungrouped to separate it. Ctrl/Alt-drag reuses it in another group. Ungrouped links and links to notes are informational.

Arrange and annotate

Drop a box beside another to join its co-premises, below it to become a child, or above it to become a parent. Shift-drop avoids connecting. Placement: Free keeps boxes where you put them. Use the corner grip to resize and +/− to expand or collapse branches. A box moved among its co-premises takes its branch with it.

Implicit marks an unstated assumption; Given marks a premise taken as given. Evaluation adds statuses and comments; in the Evaluation Overview, click a note to show its box on the map, and use a note’s trash can to delete it. Review locks structural editing while allowing evaluations.

Save and share

Save to File keeps an editable JSON copy; Save As… chooses a new destination. Browser autosaves appear in Recent Maps. Check the save indicator to see whether a file is linked or the copy is browser-only. Export images for sharing, or use String Mode to edit the map as structured text. Collaborate shares a map for live editing; shared maps are stored online.

Useful shortcuts and formatting

Shortcuts apply to the selected box when you are not typing. More are shown on buttons and menus.

Toggle support / objection or rebuttalS or O
Toggle regular / weak objection or rebuttalW
Add supportEnter
Add objection / rebuttalShift+Enter
Add weak objection / rebuttalCtrl+Enter
Add co-premise right / leftTab / Shift+Tab
Add parent / noteAlt+↑ / Alt+Enter
Undo / redoCtrl+Z / Ctrl+Y
Save / save asCtrl+S save / Ctrl+Shift+S save as
Search the mapCtrl+F after clicking the map
Fit / centerZ / C
Deductive / check selected stepK / Shift+K
Derive a parent from unattached premisesShift+K
Cancel edit / open HelpEsc / /

Rich text: **bold**, *italic*, [text](url), and $…$ for LaTeX math. Rich text is off by default; enable it to use formatting.

Deductive check

Each row is one step: a premise box (with its co-premises) and the box it supports. A step is marked only when its conclusion follows from those premises by a rule this check knows, reading the sentences as written. Anything else is left unmarked — it may still be a good argument. Click a row to go to it.
